According to 2 the previously referenced SFA Pacific report, “For future IGCC with CO removal for 2 sequestration, a two-stage Selexol process presently appears to be the preferred AGR process – as indicated by ongoing engineering studies at EPRI and by various engineering firms with IGCC interests.” [66] As several vendors have indicated that Selexol is sensitive to NH and have specified that NH 3 3 should be reduced to a concentration below 10 ppmv in the syngas feed, a water wash column is included upstream of the AGR for NH control, as detailed in Section 3.1.12.1.4. 3 As shown in Exhibit 3-3, syngas enters the bottom of the first of two absorbers and flows upward through packed beds where it contacts chilled solvent—loaded with CO —entering at 2 the top of the column, which preferentially removes H S from the gas phase. 2 Exhibit 3-3. Flow diagram for a conventional two-stage AGR unit The gas from the H S absorber flows upward through the packed beds of the second absorber. 2 CO is removed from the gas phase first by semi-lean, flash-regenerated solvent entering near 2 the middle of the tower, followed by chilled, lean solvent entering at the top of the tower. The treated gas passes through de-entrainment devices at the top of the tower before exiting the 72 COST AND PERFORMANCE BASELINE FOR FOSSIL ENERGY PLANTS VOLUME 1: BITUMINOUS COAL AND NATURAL GAS TO ELECTRICITY absorber and being sent directly to the CT. A portion of the gas can also be used for coal drying, when required. The CO loaded solvent exits the CO absorber. A portion is sent to the H S absorber, which is 2 2 2 pumped up to pressure and then chilled prior to reaching the H S absorber, and the remainder 2 is sent to a series of flash drums for regeneration. The portion sent to the flash regeneration is expanded in the HP CO recycle flash drum at 2.0 2 MPa (289.7 psia) where H , CH , CO , and other dissolved gases are transferred to the gas 2 4 2 phase. The flashed off gas is compressed and returned to the CO absorber, minimizing product 2 losses to the CO stream. 2 The amount of H recovered from the syngas stream is dependent on the Selexol process design 2 conditions. In this report, H recovery is 99.5 percent per pass. The minimal H slip to the CO 2 2 2 sequestration stream maximizes the overall plant efficiency.
